prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms free of Doppler and recoil shifts to inter-laboratory-verified fractional uncertainties at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B015 alone, credited to Katori and Ye. Having read the full exchange and the chair's questions, I can now answer the lineage question in one sentence. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool for counting optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, including single-ion clocks. The lattice clock is different in kind. The magic-wavelength condition cancels the differential light shift, so that thousands of neutral atoms are held Doppler- and recoil-free and interrogated in parallel. That removes the statistical limit that bounds a single ion and led to the 10^-18 regime. As a theorist who works with experimentalists, I find the strongest evidence is that the systematics are understood term by term (blackbody radiation, lattice light shifts, collisions) and that independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree when compared directly. The regime has opened observations that were not possible before, such as gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, tighter limits on the drift of constants and dark-matter searches. For the citation I support the wording above: it names the scheme and the 10^-18 regime, and it does not mention the redefinition of the second. I treat that redefinition as timing and not as evidence, so I do not think it argues for waiting a year. Waiting would only add the risk that the credited pair is overtaken by events. I do not want a second part. Adding any three-name entry would break the three-person limit, and a one-name part such as B040 is not defensible on the record I can see.
statement.case_against: The reservation I cannot remove is that most of the supporting argument is about precision and capability, and the statute rewards a discovery or an invention. I defend the lattice clock as an invention, but a committee member who takes a narrow view of discovery could reasonably place a new phenomenon first, such as the moire flat bands of B017 or the topological insulators of B051. Neither of these is incoherent as a prize, and both are younger as physics than B015 is as a measurement tool. Second, a two-name credit cannot capture the contributions of the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, of Lemonde and of Lemke and Ludlow, and I have no independent means of weighing them. The citation can say 'the optical lattice clock' without claiming more than the pair did, but the exclusion remains. Third, the case is partly about what is still ahead, since the second has not been redefined.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B051 (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan) as a genuine new state of matter with independent confirmation, and he concedes that the credit is the weak point and that he would support B015 if it cannot be resolved.
responses.response: I accept your core point that the prize is for a discovery or invention and not for a record number, and I have kept B051 as one of my alternatives for that reason. The science is firm, and I do not doubt fifteen years of reproduction in transport and ARPES. Where I disagree is on the credit. Mele is inseparable from Kane in the original theory, and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal guided the Molenkamp experiment, so a trio of Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan leaves out people the record puts at the centre. A pair of Katori and Ye does not carry an equally sharp internal split, and no member has proposed a different pair. If you and Mehlig can fix the credit within three names, I would listen, but I would not move B051 above B015 on today's record.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B017 (MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer) as a theory-plus-experiment door-opener with wide reproduction, and she says she would not oppose B015 if the committee prefers a metrology prize.
responses.response: I take the door-opener argument seriously, and in my own field the flat-band theory followed by the 2018 experiment is a model of how a prize case should look. I put B017 as an alternative because of this. I weigh your unresolved-credit point and the open pairing mechanism more heavily than you do. Yuan Cao, the Dean and Young groups and the Santos, Lopes dos Santos and Peres theory are outside the three names, and the platform is still moving. The lattice clock has its own reservations, but it has settled systematics and verified agreement between laboratories. I would suggest that B017 is the stronger candidate a few years from now, and not that it is the weaker science.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes make lattice clocks a tool and not a discovery, and he discloses a year in John Hall's Boulder laboratory, which touches the JILA group of Jun Ye.
responses.response: I think the lineage objection is answered by the sentence I gave above, which rests on the magic-wavelength scheme and many-atom interrogation and not on the comb or on ion control. I would ask you and Lindroth to test that wording, since you know the precision-spectroscopy literature better than I do. I note your Boulder disclosure and agree that the committee should record it. It is a tradition-level connection with no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and it does not change my assessment. In the same spirit I repeat that I have no tie to either credited name.

responses.point: Danielsson proposes B015 plus B040 as a three-laureate prize, and he concedes that a single name for IceCube is the weakest part.
responses.response: I follow the logic of pairing a laboratory measurement with an observational discovery, and I agree that IceCube opened a real window. I would not follow you to a second part. As you say yourself, one credited name for a collaboration of this scale, with AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES outside it, is hard to defend, and I defer to you and Pearce on how firm the source identifications are. The three-person limit leaves no room for a better-credited second part next to Katori and Ye. A single-part prize with a clear citation seems to me better than a compromise whose weakest element we already know.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether a metrology achievement should be weighed as a discovery, whether to await the redefinition of the second, and whether a second part would be both distinct and balanced.
responses.response: On timing I would not wait. The performance at 10^-18 has already been demonstrated and compared between laboratories, and the redefinition depends on metrological and political steps that are outside our assessment of the science. On a second part I agree with your own doubt, since Zoller and Cirac recur across B011 and B016 and the three-person limit leaves too little room. I am glad to help with the citation text if you and Kroll draft it. I would want the sentence about what is new relative to 2005 and 2012 to appear explicitly in the committee's motivation, so that the lineage question is answered on the record.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the optical lattice clock as an invention distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, or whether a majority will read it as a quantitative step in precision.
Whether the contributions of NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other clock groups are adequately reflected by naming only Katori and Ye. I cannot weigh this independently of an external expert report.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second is better treated as irrelevant to this decision or as a reason to wait. I currently treat it as timing only.
Whether B017 or B051 would be easier to defend as a discovery than B015 if the credit issues were resolved. I defer to Olsson and Eriksson on materials physics.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with superconducting-circuit groups at Chalmers, so I am close to B012 (circuit QED) and, more broadly, to B011 in the quantum-computing community. I would recuse myself or defer on those candidates, and for that reason I no longer list B012 as an alternative. I have no collaboration, funding or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or their groups, and none to the credited names in B017 or B051. Olsson and I are both at Chalmers, which is an institutional connection and not tied to any candidate. I note Kroll's Boulder disclosure and Danielsson's cosmology interest as recorded in the chair's summary.
